subtype: Approach: recording a practice and noticing mistakes [Revision]
passage: Note from Suraj's mother, evening. Suraj asked to borrow my phone and took it to his room. When I looked in, he was recording his speech for the school assembly, then playing it back with a frown. "I sound like a train," he said. "And I mumble the last words." He wrote 'pause' in the margin after every sentence and tried again. His little brother Mohit giggled outside the door, but Suraj ignored him. He recorded it a second time and listened. "Better," he said, "I can hear every word." He seemed relieved, and asked for the phone again in the morning.

qa.q: What did Suraj write in the margin after every sentence?
qa.a: Suraj wrote 'pause' in the margin after every sentence.

qa.q: How did Suraj feel after listening to the second recording?
qa.a: Suraj was relieved and satisfied, since every word could be heard and he asked for the phone again in the morning.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Suraj use to improve, and why?
qa.a: Suraj could practise in front of a small audience or ask a family member to signal when he speeds up. Live feedback adds to what a recording shows.

qa.q: How might Mohit see Suraj's practice?
qa.a: Mohit giggled outside the door and was ignored, so Mohit may see it as funny, or may feel left out of the serious work.

grounding: A boy records his speech on his mother's phone, notices he speaks too fast and mumbles the end, then pauses after each sentence and re-records to compare.

subtype: Approach: recording a practice and noticing mistakes [Revision]
passage:
Friday
Today I recorded my speech for the Science Day assembly on Mummy's phone, just to hear it. BIG mistake. Or maybe not. I sounded like a train with no brakes. And at the end of each sentence my voice went down into a mumble. Suraj bhaiya listened and said, "What was that last word, little brother? Mmmmfff?" I was annoyed, but he was right. So I tried again. This time I paused after every sentence, counted one in my head, and said the last word as loudly as the first. Then I played both recordings one after the other. The second one sounded like a real speech. I'm going to do it once more tomorrow.
- Harish

qa.q: Whose phone did Harish record the speech on?
qa.a: Harish recorded it on Mummy's phone.

qa.q: How did Harish feel when Suraj bhaiya joked about the last word?
qa.a: Harish felt annoyed but also knew the joke was fair, which pushed the change.

qa.q: What else could Harish do to check his speech besides recording?
qa.a: Harish could give the speech to Suraj bhaiya and ask him to raise a hand whenever it gets too fast.

qa.q: How does the recording look to Suraj bhaiya?
qa.a: Suraj bhaiya finds the mumbling funny but his teasing points out a real problem he can hear clearly.

grounding: It shows a boy recording a speech, noticing he talks too fast and mumbles endings, pausing more and re-recording to compare.

subtype: Approach: recording a practice and noticing mistakes [Revision]
passage: In the small school at Nandgaon, Manjula ma'am had chosen Wasim to give the welcome speech on Independence Day. Two evenings before, Wasim borrowed his mother's phone and recorded himself in the courtyard, with hens clucking in the background. When he played it back, he frowned. He was racing, and the end of every sentence disappeared. "Wel-come-to-our-guests-mmm." His Ammi laughed from the doorway, and he laughed too. He tried again, slowly, stopping to breathe after each sentence and ending each one clearly. He played the two recordings back to back. The second sounded like a grown-up. The next day he showed Manjula ma'am both, and she said, "Now I can hear every word."

qa.a: He recorded himself in the courtyard, with hens clucking.

qa.q: How did Wasim feel when he first played back the recording?
qa.a: He was surprised and a little embarrassed at how fast it was, then able to laugh at it.

qa.q: What else could Wasim do if he had no phone to record on?
qa.a: He could say the speech to Ammi and ask her to tap the table when he rushes or mumbles.

qa.q: How does the change look to Manjula ma'am?
qa.a: Manjula ma'am is pleased, since she can now hear every word of the speech.

grounding: It shows a boy recording his speech, noticing he speaks too fast and mumbles, pausing after sentences and re-recording to compare.
